newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMS II important for further convergence-Tietmeyer.
newsitem.headline: EMS II important for further convergence-Tietmeyer.

text.p: Nations remaining outside Europe's currency union at its inception should be linked in some other way to signal interest in increasing convergence, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said on Friday.

Acknowledging that it was highly unlikely that all 15 European nations could join the European Economic and Monetary Union at its launch in 1999, Tietmeyer urged non-participants to join a so-called EMS II system at that time.

"EMS II can generate a very important signal," Tietmeyer said, adding "What the signal must be is: all countries - whether they are already participants in monetary union or not - want to strengthen convergence."
After all "convergence is the objective of monetary integration, beyond the inception of monetary union," Tietmeyer said in a text prepared for delivery at a banking congress.
While the EMS II was generally considered to be a good idea, Tietmeyer said "I regret that, the way things are going, participation will presumably be on a voluntary basis only."
The new common currency, the Euro, will become the anchor currency for EMS II, taking over for the mark which is defacto the anchor currency for the EMS, Tietmeyer said.

But he highlighted a major difference between the two anchor currencies, noting that while the mark could have been removed from its position, the Euro's "de jure role is defined by the system itself."
Consequently, the standards for the Euro are much higher than they were for the mark, Tietmeyer said, adding "The Euro must safeguard domestic stability, or the entire system will start to totter."
"This includes, in the event of a conflict, giving domestic monetary stability priority over external exchange rate stability," he added.
Tietmeyer said stable exchange rates are important, but cautioned that these must be based on solid economic fundamentals.

While Tietmeyer said central bank intervention is often not successful and could dangerously inflate the money stock of the strong currency nation, it should be kept in the arsenal of policy instruments at the future European central bank.
Intervention, which central banks have in the past used to guide currencies into a certain direction, can in certain cases "generate signals," Tietmeyer said.
Tietmeyer also encouraged nations, whose central rate may be too ambitious, to devalue their currencies without fear of losing prestige.
"Conversely, neither should a phobia evolve in the euro area, regarding any devaluation against the euro as an unfair, malicious act," Tietmeyer said.
